fichas.title: Student Residences: General Design Notes
fichas.summary: Student residences near colleges and universities may be organized as courtyard groups, open structures, or larger buildings. Their communal areas are important to acceptance. Design guidance covers minimum room requirements, accessibility, escape routes, recommended living-space areas, and shared or individual-room arrangements.
uses: Student accommodation for the duration of a course

dimensions.ocr_raw:
STUDENT RESIDENCES
General Design Notes

Halls of residence are normally provided near colleges and
universities for students and are normally built and operated in
various architectural forms (20-30 units in courtyard layout or
groups of open structures, large buildings with 80 or more units).
They are used for the accommodation of students for the duration
of their course. The size and equipping of the rooms is often
very limited. Options such as single rooms, (double) flats and flat
sharing groups have proved successful. The arrangement and
design of the communal areas within and around the residences
are decisive for their acceptance.

Ground floor plan

Section A-A

0 Student residence in Halle/Saale

Arch.: Gemot Schulz
in: Hillebrand!+ Schulz, Cologne

Requirements
Student flats are 'living places' and not considered as residential
homes in the sense of the building regulations. The general
requirements of the building regulations essentially concern
residential rooms with minimum requirements for floor area (8 m2),
ceiling height (2.40 m), orientation, ventilation and lighting (window
area Ys of the room area), accessibility requirements (i.e. for disabled
people) and escape routes (two independent escape routes from
each floor, one of which is a legally essential stairway). The state
guidelines for student residences set recommended dimensions
for living places (approx. 12 m2 for single rooms and approx. 16
m2 for flats). In addition to this, a certain area will be required for
communal use.
Forms of living
These can be categorised into flat sharing -> f) individual rooms->
0.

e-

0

and

When flats are shared, the communal area is of more importance,
similar to a home. A group of rooms (4-8) with some functions
transferred to the communal area (kitchen, bathroom) has a
linear -> f) or central -> 8 type of layout. Single rooms located
along a corridor with communal bathroom and kitchen form the
classic (but anonymous) form of student residence. What has
proved successful is the further development of the single room
as flat->
(room with shower room and perhaps kitchenette) and
the double flat -> 0 - 0 (two rooms with communal kitchen and
bath). This latter form of residence can be used very flexibly by
singles and also by couples (with child).

fichas.title: Shared Student Flats
fichas.summary: Shared flats group several rooms around communal functions such as a kitchen and bathroom. The communal area may be arranged linearly or centrally. The illustrated shared flat has single rooms, communal bathrooms, and a central communal kitchen.

fichas.title: Flat and Double-Flat Layouts
fichas.summary: The illustrated individual flat includes a shower room and may include a kitchenette. The double flat consists of two rooms with a communal kitchen and bathroom and can accommodate singles or couples, including a couple with a child. A further plan shows a double flat with communal bathroom, kitchen, and cupboard zone.
